subject: Geography
title: Living with the Climate
learningOutcomes: Describe how climate shapes the lifestyle of people in coastal areas, plains, deserts, polar and tropical regions.
Compare and contrast the lifestyle of people living in polar regions with those living in tropical regions.
Investigate examples of extreme weather on Earth, their reasons and the conditions that accompany them.
Recall the causes of climate change and explain how global warming and climate change are related.
Explain the impact of climate change on Pakistan and the individual, national and international actions that prevent global warming.

sections.heading: Climate and Lifestyles
sections.body: People living in different climatic zones adopt different lifestyles. The world map shows six climate zones — Polar, Subpolar, Temperate, Subtropical, Tropical and Equatorial. Comparing a population map with the climate map shows that people tend to settle where the climate is favourable. Coastal areas hold the world's largest cities (New York, Boston, Shanghai, Mumbai, Karachi) because they offer jobs, natural resources and ports for trade; their key activities are fish farming and trade — the Blue Economy — supported by mangroves and coral reefs.

sections.heading: Plains and Deserts
sections.body: Plains are flat areas of land with warm summers and cold winters, where most people practise agriculture and ranching. The Indus plains are depositional flood plains formed with silt, giving Punjab and Sindh fertile soil; the buffalo is the main resource of food, clothing and shelter. The deserts east of the Indus are home to Rajput, Baloch and Dravidian people, whose houses are made of unbaked bricks, wood and straw. Thar life is based on the joint family system, with men ploughing and grazing while women fetch water and do household work.

sections.heading: Polar and Tropical Regions
sections.body: Polar regions have extremely harsh weather with long winter nights and long summer days; millions live in the Arctic but Antarctica has only researchers. People wear six to seven layers, keep toes and fingers warm, travel by aircraft or sledge and eat dried food to save fuel. Dudinka (Yenisei River, 20,000 people, −33°C in January) and Harbin (the Chinese 'ice city', 10 million people) are examples. The tropics are warm all year (25–28°C) with two seasons; about one third of the world's people live there. The Amazon Basin (≈5 million km², nine countries) is home to the Kayapo tribe, who practise slash-and-burn farming of bananas, manioc and rice.

sections.heading: Extreme Weather Events
sections.body: Extreme weather events are unusual, unexpected, severe or unseasonal occurrences — cyclones, heat waves, cold waves, thunderstorms, wildfires and dust storms — that cause health problems, loss of life, economic costs, droughts, floods, landslides and ecosystem changes. Each event is accompanied by particular conditions: thunderstorms bring thunder, lightning and heavy rain; blizzards bring heavy snow, cold and wind; dust storms bring wind, clouds and arid conditions; ice storms bring freezing rain, ice and cold. A single lightning bolt can carry up to one billion volts.

sections.heading: Climate Change – Causes and Impacts
sections.body: Weather is made of air, water and heat. Climate change is the long-term alteration of temperatures and weather patterns, caused since the 1800s mostly by burning fossil fuels, which release greenhouse gases that trap heat. This raises Earth's overall temperature — global warming — producing stronger storms, bigger cyclones and atmospheric rivers that carry moisture up to 2,000 km. Rain is 'violent' above 5 cm/hour; La Réunion received 1.8 m in two days in 1966 (Cyclone Denise). Global warming has cut wildlife by 69% in under 50 years (WWF 2022), a sixth mass extinction, and the impact is most daunting in the Hindu Kush–Himalaya region.

sections.heading: Impact on Pakistan & Prevention
sections.body: Pakistan has more than 7,200 glaciers — the most outside the poles — which are melting faster and causing more, and more severe, floods; the Indus empties into the Arabian Sea, cholera can spread in floods, and crop failure brings food scarcity, poverty and urbanisation. Rising seas erode the Indus Delta and raise salinity. Prevention works at three levels: individuals save energy, use public transport, save food, apply the 3Rs and use renewables; nations cut fossil fuels, tax polluters, subsidise clean energy, decarbonise and retrofit buildings; and internationally, the Paris Agreement (December 2015) set a target to reduce the world's average temperature by two degrees.

definitions.definition: Coastal economic activity based on fish farming and sea trade.
Flood plains built up from silt deposited by a river during floods.
The increase in the overall temperature of the Earth.
Long-term alterations in temperatures and weather patterns.
Gases from burning fossil fuels that trap more heat than Earth needs.
Narrow channels in the air that carry moisture up to 2,000 km, causing intense rain or snow.
Reducing one's carbon footprint, mainly CO₂ and methane emissions.
Slash-and-burn clearing of forest for crops, as in the Amazon Basin.
Unusual, unexpected, severe or unseasonal weather occurrences.
The first climate treaty (December 2015), aiming to cut world temperature by two degrees.

examTips: Remember the three prevention levels in order: Individual → National → International.
Don't confuse global warming (rising temperature) with climate change (long-term change in weather patterns) — global warming is the main cause of climate change.
Learn the polar-vs-tropical comparison: harsh cold, layered clothing and dried food vs warm all year, two seasons and slash-and-burn farming.
